power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Preterm born children (preterms) are at elevated likelihood for social-communicative and language difficulties.
No study before has investigated the longitudinal development of early joint attention (JA) behaviours in preterms.
We examined early JA development and the relation with later language abilities in preterms.
This prospective longitudinal study examined the early JA development in 51 preterms with a gestational age below 30 weeks.
The Early Social Communication Scales (ESCS) were administered at the corrected ages of 10, 18 and 24 months, and coded for infants' JA behaviours and coordinated vocalisations.
At 36 months, receptive and expressive language abilities were evaluated by the Mullen Scales of Early Learning.
Most JA behaviours (basic or advanced, with or without coordinated vocalisations) developed between 10 and 18 months, while basic initiating JA behaviours showed a decrease during this age period.
Responding to JA (RJA) was the only skill with a continued increase in frequency between 18 and 24 months.
Advanced IJA behaviours at 10 months and increases towards 24 months emerged as predictor of both language skills.
Initial level and increases in RJA predicted receptive language.
JA development in preterms, as measured with the ESCS, mainly occurs between 10 and 18 months, but there was substantial inter-individual heterogeneity in JA development.
Frequency of advanced IJA behaviours appears to contribute more to later language than initiating behavioural requests, possibly because these behaviours elicit more language learning opportunities.
Initial level and improvements in RJA and advanced IJA throughout the second year of life may benefit language development.
The previous version of this preprint no longer accurately reflects the study's findings.
During the revision process, an error was identified in the dataset.
Correcting this error resulted in changes to the study's results and conclusions.

Readers are therefore referred to the accepted manuscript, which contains the corrected analyses and conclusions: https://eur03.safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fdoi.org%2F10.1016%2Fj.infbeh.2026.102263&data=05%7C02%7CHanna.VandeVyver%40UGent.be%7Cfdc7f9db090b40f4f62008df2ec028cd%7Cd7811cdeecef496c8f91a1786241b99c%7C1%7C0%7C639281074992489066%7CUnknown%7CTWFpbGZsb3d8eyJFbXB0eU1hcGkiOnRydWUsIlYiOiIwLjAuMDAwMCIsIlAiOiJXaW4zMiIsIkFOIjoiTWFpbCIsIldUIjoyfQ%3D%3D%7C0%7C%7C%7C&sdata=sn8o%2B7p2iMBvCMHFkp4aJQoT4w4Pb8S%2BFMFQzzu2Sws%3D&reserved=0.
